blocks.text: And the brook כרית Cerith is named from the verb כרה cara, which the Greek translators at Iob. XL, 25. render very aptly by ἐνσιτεῖσθαι [ensiteisthai], that is, to be fed or to eat, because at it the Prophet was miraculously fed by ravens. If this conjecture is true, a prolepsis [col. 217] must be recognized in these words: Hide thyself by the brook Cerith. However that may be, from the sacred text we know this much: that this brook was near the Jordan, and to the east of Samaria. So Josephus was not paying attention when he wrote that Elias withdrew εἰς τὰ πρὸς νότον μέρη [eis ta pros noton merē], to the parts that lie towards the south ^{(5)}. And far more absurdly Eutychius, confusing this retreat of Elias with his forty-day fast on Mount Horeb: وهرب ايلياس النبي علي تخوم الاردن الي جبل حوريب وهو طور سينا وسكن في شعب عين وكان يشرب الما من ذلك الشعب [wa-haraba Īliyās al-nabī ʿalī tukhūm al-Urdunn ilī jabal Ḥūrīb wa-huwa Ṭūr Sīnā wa-sakana fī shiʿb ʿayn wa-kāna yashrabu al-mā min dhālika al-shiʿb] And Elias the prophet fled through the borders of the Jordan to Mount Horeb, which is Mount Sinai, and dwelt by the cleft of a spring, from which he drank water. To these words he adds the rest about the raven bringing bread and meat.
